newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.S. rights group urges Jordan to repeal press law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rights group urges Jordan to repeal press law.

text.p: A U.S.-based human rights group urged Jordan on Friday to repeal sweeping curbs on reporting introduced a few months before parliamentary elections.

Human Rights Watch/Middle East said in a report that the amended law imposed arbitrary restrictions and exorbitant punishments on journalists and seemed more concerned with gagging criticism than protecting national interests.

"In the absence of compelling justifications by the government of Jordan, Human Rights Watch finds the restrictions on expression in the press law amendments create unacceptable infringements on the right to free expression," it said.

The amended law, unveiled three weeks ago, bans items which offend the king and royal family, contain contempt of religion, damage national unity, encourage crime, undermine confidence in the Jordanian dinar or offend public morals.
It also prevents journalists from writing about Jordan's armed forces and security services without special permission.
The bans cover cartoons, pictures and articles. Fines for violators were raised to at least 15,000 dinars ($21,200) from 1,000 dinars. Offending newspapers can be suspended.
King Hussein said on Thursday the law was needed to stop some journalists from "harming the nation, or mocking national interests and unity" and said it would not be revoked.
"Freedom has its limits," he told an audience in the southern town of Kerak.
Human Rights Watch -- in the report titled "Jordan: A death knell for free expression?" -- said the press law was aimed at imposing a regime of self-censorship in Jordan.

It said many of the restrictions "seem designed to bar news and critical reporting about government officials and institutions, and the conduct of foreign and domestic policy, rather than to protect national security."
The law would limit the openness of parliamentary elections due to be held in November, despite pledges from Interior Minister Nazir Rasheed they would be free and fair, it added.

"The interior minister did not explain how free and fair elections can take place when the government has imposed harsh restrictions on the flow of information in newspapers and other publications about issues of broad concern to voters," it said.
"The content bans are arbitrary by two measures: the necessity for such sweeping restrictions has not been demonstrated, and the measures appear disproportionate."
